reviewer_concerns.concern_text: An extensive methodological approach is provided for both the training and testing datasets. The training dataset uses a method for automatic classification developed by one of the co-authors (PWM), i.e. the Uni-G. Why was an external EKG classification tool not compared? Can you provide some justification for the significant reliance on this software for label generation?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that Uni-G software is not directly used for generating the test dataset and the final classification is based entirely on the decisions of certified cardiologists; for training and validation it is used for cleaning and improving the quality of labelling, avoiding possible mistakes by the cardiologists.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There should be better empirical reasoning for why 98% of the dataset was used for training, furthermore why 827 samples were selected for the test. There needs to be more details highlighted about the distribution of these classes in the training, validation and test sets.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors justified the 98/2 split by analogy to large-dataset DL benchmarks (e.g. Wikitext-103 99.5/0.21/0.24 split) and noted the test set was small because it required more demanding annotation; class distributions were added to Supplementary Table 3.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: While lines 271 through 282 reflect highly optimistic views of the work, there should be some caution when issuing states such as 'state of the art, leading to widespread use etc.' The authors are certainly commended for the work in developing the dataset, and for demonstrating this 'proof of concept' study, however due to a lack of external validation with other arrhythmia detection models these broad statements are premature.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors agreed and softened the conclusion to a proof-of-concept claim, rewriting the final paragraph of the Discussion to remove overly optimistic claims.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: No error bars and confidence intervals are provided. It is standard practice to go train a network several times to determine the influence of the random seed used for training. Without such information, it is impossible to tell if the results are spurious or not. The authors must provide a measure of variance of their results.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors trained the neural network 10 times with the same hyperparameters and different initializations; added shaded performance bands in Figure 1 showing the range and chose a model with mAP immediately above median.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Insufficient description of the model selection process. The authors used a very similar network architecture as in [4] but they do not describe how they selected their final network. In particular, it is unclear which hyperparameters were considered (learning rates, optimizers, activation functions, number of neurons, number of layers, kernel sizes), nor how the hyperparameters were selected (manual, grid search, or model-based approach).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added a new subsection on hyperparameter tuning in Methods but declined to provide direct performance comparison because architecture and hyperparameters were tuned in parallel with dataset improvements.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is a very high discrepancy between number of training and test samples (0.03%). A typical split would be 8:1:1 for training, validation and test. Having an additional test set to compare to experts is desirable but currently this set is tiny and the values in the results tables only stem from one cardiology resident, one emergency resident and one medical student. The authors should provide more details on that.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors noted that two of each annotator type were used, justified the 98/2 split by reference to large-dataset practice, and added boxplots of bootstrapped F1 under 90/5/5 random, by-date, and by-patient stratified splits in the Editor-requested rebuttal. Reviewer in Round 2 remained partly unsatisfied: 'my concern with the low numbers in the test-set is still a factor. A follow-up validation set may be warranted.'

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Please provide additional experiments where your model is trained on 90% of the data, validated on 5%, and performance is reported on the remaining 5% test data. A stratified split in which all traces from one individual go together in one of the folds or splits should be used. Additionally, a time-split in which the traces are sorted by their date of recording (90% earliest, next 5% validation, newest 5% test) should be used so that prospective use of the method can be simulated. Finally, inter-rater reliability should be reported for the comparison of human and model performance on the final set of 827 traces.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors ran the requested 90/5/5 analyses under random, by-date, and by-patient stratified splits on 2,322,513 records; reported bootstrapped F1 boxplots in Figure 6 and added Table 6(b) on inter-rater reliability.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: ECG signal classification (multi-class abnormalities); modality is borderline (signal time-series, not pure imaging). Included because reviewer concerns map cleanly to MLGG dimensions (split protocol, sample size, CI/variance, hyperparameter selection). Has 2 review rounds plus editor-mediated additional split-protocol experiments.

Editorial note states manuscript was previously reviewed at another journal not operating transparent peer review; prior referee reports redacted. Only post-revision comments from Reviewer #2 present (non-substantive thanks/encouragement). Reviewers #1 and #3 marked 'None'. No substantive methodology concerns extractable.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I believe there should be more discussion on alternative input-based saliency techniques (e.g. DeepLIFT, SHAP, integrated gradients, etc.) and why deep Taylor decomposition was chosen as the technique presented in this manuscript. Further, there should be a more detailed description of related work in this area, as applying these techniques to healthcare data is not exactly novel.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added a new section 'Explaining predictions in other ways' discussing alternative saliency attribution methods (Gradient x Input, Integrated Gradients, DeepLIFT, vanilla LRP, LIME, SHAP) and explained that for their ReLU-only network with no additive bias these methods are largely equivalent at intermediate layers.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: On page 2, the authors state that explanation 'quality was assessed by manual inspection of trained specialists (medical doctors) in emergency medicine', but this is not mentioned again or expounded upon for the remainder of the manuscript. Did clinicians agree or disagree with, did they find them helpful, etc.? These are very important questions for a study like this.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors described an iterative development process with ED clinicians but did not provide quantitative inter-rater agreement; deferred formal evaluation to future work.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The outcome prevalence rates are very low (2.44%, 0.75%, 1.68%). The authors should explain whether any techniques were used to account for this (loss weighting, resampling, etc.)
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors tried oversampling with replacement for the positive class; reported it did not significantly affect model performance but did stretch output probabilities; final results were computed without resampling.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Given the authors' discussions of sensitivity and specificity tradeoffs in baseline models, it would be nice to see sensitivity and specificity results for their framework as well. I would argue that these statistics could be equally important as feature attribution assignment for clinician trust.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors declined to add sensitivity/specificity, citing that choice of operating point is subjective and that since their model dominates ROC/PR-space it dominates at all operating points.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Given (1) the authors' focus on critical illness, (2) the hospital mortality statistic presented in Extended Table 2, and (3) the basis target for the SOFA score being in-hospital mortality, it is a little perplexing why in-hospital mortality was not included as an outcome of interest. I think the rationale behind choosing outcomes should be expanded upon.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors agreed that in-hospital mortality is an interesting endpoint but chose to focus on exacerbation of disease for the most frequent hospitalization causes; left mortality for future work.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Regarding the cross-validation setup: it would be best if the authors could clarify their setup, whether it is a standard cross-validation + hold-out setup, or a nested cross-validation process.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added a paragraph in Discussion describing 5-fold cross-validation with 80% train / 10% val / 10% test per fold; all data for a single patient was assigned to either train, validation or test (patient-level isolation confirmed). Added Supplementary Figure 1 illustrating the CV scheme.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: ALI is obsolete: we abandoned it several years ago, to include ALI in ARDS (it is equivalent to mild ARDS).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that ALI ground truth was based on the need for CPAP or NIV during admission because PaO2/FiO2 measurements were not available; ALI onset was defined as the first occurrence of NIV or CPAP.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: EHR ICU time-series for sepsis/AKI/ALI prediction — squarely in MLGG scope. Reviewer 2 was minimal/positive; substantive concerns from Reviewer 1 (interpretability + evaluation panel) and Reviewer 3 (outcome definition). Authors used 5-fold CV with patient-level split. Reviewer 1 had a few unresolved items (clinician assessment quantification, sens/spec).

Pure histopathology WSI (whole-slide image) gastric cancer detection using DeepLab v3 segmentation; modality explicitly excluded from MLGG scope (CLAUDE.md: 'unsupported modality boundary: 不覆盖组学 (TCGA/scRNA/GWAS)、影像'). Reviewer concerns are dominated by histology-specific topics (WSI labelling, IHC, scanner robustness, pixel-level annotation, stain normalization). No substantive concerns map cleanly to MLGG's retrospective-EHR-binary-classification framework.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Title is actually not conform TRIPOD, it should mention that the study develops and validates a prediction model.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors renamed the manuscript to 'Performing risk stratification for COVID-19 mortality when individual level data is not available – development and validation of a prediction model'.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: You used default hyperparameters for the gradient boosting model. Why, and can you specify what the hyperparameters are?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors said default hyperparameters consistently provide good performance with large populations and many outcomes; the full list is long so they added a reference to LightGBM's parameter documentation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The outcome: now the authors write '6 weeks prior to the extraction date to allow sufficient time for the outcome to occur' and in the next paragraph 'death during a hospitalization following a new covid-19 infection'. The latter is a clear definition, but I am wondering whether there were no cases who were still alive and hospitalized at May 30th? I would think there are, and this has to be mentioned.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors re-ran the analysis allowing for full 3 months of follow-up (extraction July 16, cases through April 16); reported that 11 of 4,179 patients (0.3%) were still hospitalized at extraction date and were not deemed recovered.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: About the newly added sensitivity analysis: (a) this was done using the recalibrated predictions based on CFR, right? (b) Please provide a more specific definition of severe disease than 'resources such as ventilators and ICU beds', including when the classification into severe or not was made. (c) I am not a fan of this post hoc analysis (the project starts with a proxy outcome, recalibrates it for mortality, and then checks performance for yet another outcome).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors confirmed sensitivity analysis used predictions recalibrated for mortality; rewrote severity definition citing NIH guidelines updated daily; acknowledged the post-hoc framing was added in response to another reviewer.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Hospitalization total duration: this variable has a different label in Table 1, but the scale is still missing. Also, I hope this does not refer to the hospitalization for covid-19. If so, that would make the whole model invalid. Please clarify.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors corrected the variable name to 'Duration of hospitalizations' (days), clarified that baseline covariates were extracted in the year prior to February 1, 2020 (before pandemic); explicitly stated 'no measurements or events (including hospitalizations) that occurred after the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic in Israel were included as predictors' and added a Table 1 footnote on this.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the version with track changes, Figure 4 has not changed. The calibration and decision curve must surely look different now that more data was added. Please check that the correct versions are used.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained software version-comparison feature failed to tag the change but the figure was updated; included all three submission versions of calibration/decision curve side-by-side for comparison.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: COVID-19 mortality risk prediction from EHR tabular features (LightGBM with SHAP) — squarely in MLGG scope. Reviewer Ben Van Calster (KU Leuven) is a known TRIPOD/PROBAST expert; concerns focus on outcome definition, future-information leakage, calibration, and decision curves. Only one substantive review round visible; Reviewer #2 satisfied without comments.

Ultrasound image-based transfer learning radiomics (Inception V3 backbone) for thyroid lymph-node metastasis prediction. Modality (medical imaging) explicitly out of MLGG scope. Reviewer concerns are radiomics/imaging-specific (probe sectioning, image quality, TIRADS labels, deep CNN baselines). No EHR/clinical-tabular leakage concerns extractable.

Chest CT image-based deep learning (ResNet152 + GradCAM) for COVID-19 diagnosis with paired CXR fusion. Pure medical imaging modality, out of MLGG scope (omics/imaging boundary). Concerns are mostly CT/CXR-specific (slice averaging, segmentation pre-processing, scanner domain). The single retraining-on-external-data concern (point 12) is methodologically interesting but applies to image-based external validation, not to MLGG's EHR-tabular framework.

Multi-omics (mRNA expression, miRNA expression, gene mutation, protein expression, transcriptomic) across 26 TCGA cancer types for irAE prediction. Omics modality explicitly out of MLGG scope (CLAUDE.md: 'omics 走 Scanpy/limma/PLINK 原生工具链'). Reviewer 2 raises classical biostat issues (univariate variable selection in n<<p, multicollinearity, FDR method) but these concerns target high-dimensional omics analysis, not EHR retrospective cohorts.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Please look at the following outcomes and not only progression: ICU admission, Mechanical ventilation, LOS, Crude and attributable mortality.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added clinical outcomes including requiring mechanical ventilation, ICU admission, and death in both derivation and validation cohorts (Table 1); hospital length of stay and viral shedding duration added in Table 2; bacterial co-infection comparison added in Supplementary Table 1.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors combine their severe category with the critical category for analysis (line 141). This combination detracts severely from the value of the analysis. By their definitions, severe patients would likely be treated on a general medicine unit while critical would be ICU patients, with very different intervention needs. Any prognostic benefit of a score is therefore lost by this combination.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors agreed and stopped combining severe and critical COVID-19 as a single category in the revised manuscript (line 111-122).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Major limitations include the following: Lack of validation in an independent population.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors enrolled an external validation cohort (from 2 hospitals in Yueyang and Shaoyang, Hunan); supplemented missing values in derivation cohort and established a nomogram based on multivariate logistic regression; the nomogram showed good calibration and discrimination in both cohorts.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Abstract should specify the number of cases included. Should specify that the cohort was retrospective. Line 72- should indicate this was retrospective evaluation.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors rewrote the Abstract section adding case numbers and study design.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Smoking history seems remarkably low compared to the prevalence of smoking in China. Is this because of incomplete data collection? How did the authors handle cases where smoking history was unknown?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the proportion was lower than national prevalence; smoking history was obtained from EMR by trained residents; cited recent reports showing similar 7-14.6% prevalence among COVID-19 patients; did not formally describe handling of unknown values.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Also, the higher severity score in those admitted more than 4 days after symptom onset is likely due to lead time bias, since it is known that the severity of disease increases until about 10 days after symptom onset. Thus, this finding does not mean that delayed admission results in greater disease severity. The authors should critically evaluate and discuss the potential role of lead time bias in contributing to their findings. Should the risk score be adjusted for days since symptom onset?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Response to this specific lead-time-bias point not fully visible in the extracted pages; the author response section primarily defends CT severity score's role in prediction.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors should compare their results with the just-published analysis Development and Validation of a Clinical Risk Score to Predict the Occurrence of Critical Illness in Hospitalized Patients With COVID-19 (JAMA Intern Med 2020). In this article, a CT severity score was not included in the final risk model, although chest radiographic abnormality remained in the model. This might be because the authors included a wider range of features (n=72) in their LASSO analysis. The authors should discuss why this difference might be.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Author response defends CT's role: 'Lung injury is the cornerstone in the pathophysiology of COVID-19... Chest CT is superior over X-ray in showing the extent and characteristics of pulmonary lesions.' Did not directly contrast LASSO feature panels with the JAMA paper.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The major weaknesses remain the clinical relevance of a prediction model heavily dependent on chest CT in healthcare systems which are actively trying to avoid this intervention. The second issue is the clinical relevance of predicting 'severe' pneumonia by their criteria.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors pointed out the limitation in the discussion (Line 415-420) about CT being used mainly for hospitalized symptomatic patients; defended CT severity score as quantitative measure of lung injury.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: COVID-19 progression prediction in moderate pneumonia using clinical + CT-severity-score features fed into multivariate logistic regression nomogram. Although the paper uses CT, the modeling is on tabular features (severity score, NLR, age, comorbidities) — closer to MLGG's clinical risk model scope than to pure image classification. Reviewer 3 raises a sharp lead-time-bias concern in round 2 that maps directly to MLGG-F02/F05. Some round-2 concerns may have been less fully resolved than authors claim.

H&E whole-slide image based deep learning (AttentionNet MIL) for breast cancer ER/PR/HER2 status determination. Pure histopathology imaging modality — out of MLGG scope. Reviewer concerns are WSI-specific (MIL attention assumption, patch averaging, TCGA cohort leave-one-out, stain variation, regional vs central ER scoring).
